title: The Pollution–Development Trap
subtitle: How environmental exposure reinforces economic underdevelopment
strapline: Poor countries breathe dirtier air, and dirty air keeps them poorer. This dashboard follows pollution and income in 159 countries since 1998 to measure each side of the loop, find who has escaped it and who is stuck, and ask what breaking it would be worth.
dek: In 35 countries with 1.45 billion people, from Nigeria to Bangladesh, fine-particle pollution is stuck high or still rising while income stays below $10,000 a head — and growth has not cleaned the air of the poorest third of countries at all. The loop runs both ways: poverty means smoky fuels and weak regulation, and pollution costs 3.7 years of life expectancy in lower-middle-income countries and erodes human capital. China turned the corner at $14,000 a head and India at about $7,000 — proof that clean air can come early, as growth policy rather than its reward.
abstract: This report tests the idea of a pollution–development trap — a loop in which poverty raises exposure to pollution and exposure in turn holds back development — with data for 159 countries with at least 1 million people. It combines population-weighted PM2.5 from satellite-based estimates (SatPM, 1998–2024) with income per head, cooking fuels, the WHO's air-pollution death rates, the World Bank's particulate damage estimates and Human Capital Index, and the causal literature on each link.

The burden falls steeply with income: the age-standardised death rate from household and ambient air pollution is 186 per 100,000 in low-income countries against 25 in high-income ones, 84% of people in low-income countries cook with polluting fuels, and PM2.5 above the WHO guideline costs an estimated 3.7 years of life expectancy in lower-middle-income countries against 0.7 in high-income ones. At the same income, each 10 µg/m³ more PM2.5 goes with a Human Capital Index about 0.02 lower (t = −7.2) and 1.3 points more child stunting.

Growth alone does not break the loop. Among the poorest third of countries by 2000 income, growth since 2000 has been unrelated to the change in PM2.5, which rose by 0.15% a year on average; in the richest third it fell 0.9% a year. Thirty-five countries with 1.45 billion people are stuck above 25 µg/m³ or still rising with incomes below $10,000 a head, and sub-Saharan Africa would reach 95% clean cooking only around 2103 at its recent pace. Yet China's pollution peaked at about $14,000 a head and has fallen by more than a third, and India's appears to have turned at about $7,000 — far earlier in development than Europe's — showing that clean air can be pursued as growth policy.

Interactive charts of the burden by income group, pollution–income trajectories, turning points, growth and pollution change, human-capital associations and clean cooking, a five-layer atlas with country cards, and an escape simulator accompany the analysis.
jel: Q53, O13, O15, I15, Q56 — air pollution; development and the environment; human resources; health and development; environment and development
method: 159 countries with at least 1 million people. PM2.5: population-weighted SatPM 1998–2024 (Washington University in St. Louis via Our World in Data), three-year averages for peaks. Income: GDP per head, PPP constant 2021 $ (WDI). Trajectory classes: cleaned up (peak ≥ 15, ≥ 25% below peak and < 20 now), turning (peak ≥ 25 before 2020, ≥ 15% below peak, ≥ 20 now), rising (≥ 20 with 2014–24 trend > +0.5%/yr, or ≥ 15 with > +1%/yr), stuck (≥ 25 otherwise), low (< 15), middle (rest); trap set = stuck or rising with GDP per head < $10,000. Burden: polluting cooking fuels (WHO via WDI), WHO 2019 age-standardised air-pollution mortality, adjusted-savings particulate damage (% GNI, 2021), Human Capital Index 2020, stunting and learning poverty (latest). Life expectancy lost = 0.098 × (PM2.5 − 5), the AQLI coefficient. Growth test by third of 2000 income: annual growth of GDP per head 2000–24 against annual change in PM2.5 2005–24. Partial associations: OLS with log GDP per head and, where stated, region fixed effects; robust t-statistics. Simulator: PM2.5 declining at a chosen annual rate to 2050; life expectancy via the AQLI coefficient; output via constant elasticities of 0.039–0.08 (Fu, Viard & Zhang 2021; Dechezleprêtre, Rivers & Stadler 2019). Associations are not causal; satellite PM2.5 includes natural dust.
author: Hunter Hughes
